title: Safe string input, capacity, truncation and termination
learningObjectives: Explain the language rule and its constraints.
Trace the example and predict its behaviour.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: Input routines must respect destination capacity and establish a valid terminator. fgets reads at most size minus one characters, then adds a null terminator when it succeeds; a newline may remain in the buffer.
understand.whyItMatters: This knowledge helps reason about C data representation, object bounds and valid memory access.
understand.analogy: Think of memory objects as labelled storage and pointers as typed references to that storage.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal pointer, lifetime and object-access rules.

explain.narrative:
Input routines must respect destination capacity and establish a valid terminator. fgets reads at most size minus one characters, then adds a null terminator when it succeeds; a newline may remain in the buffer.

Check the declared types, object lifetime, valid bounds and function preconditions before using the construct. Enable compiler warnings and test edge cases.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.code: Unbounded input can overwrite adjacent memory. Bounded input still needs a policy for detecting and handling an overlong line and for clearing the remainder of that line.

practise.guidedTask: fgets receives the buffer capacity, reads at most 31 input characters and terminates the result. strcspn finds the first newline so it can be replaced with the null terminator.
practise.independentTask: Explain why sizeof name is passed instead of a guessed large number.
hints: Read a line with a defined maximum length. Detect whether the input was truncated and handle the remaining characters deliberately.
fgets returns NULL on an input failure or when end-of-file occurs before any character is read.
A line that fills the buffer without a newline may be longer than the accepted limit.
